title: Should degrees be shorter?

turns.speaker: Gus
turns.text: They're piloting two-year degrees. Same content, three terms a year instead of two, no long summer.

turns.speaker: Mimi
turns.text: Which saves a year of living costs, and that's the real expense rather than the fees.

turns.speaker: Lorcan
turns.text: It does. My worry is what gets lost, and it isn't teaching hours.

turns.speaker: Lorcan
turns.text: The internship, the job that pays for next year, the research placement. Those all live in the summer and they're a large part of what a degree is for.

turns.speaker: Mimi
turns.text: That's a fair point and it lands differently by subject. A law student loses a vacation scheme. A maths student loses less.

turns.speaker: Gus
turns.text: There's also a maturing argument, which sounds soft and probably isn't nothing.

turns.speaker: Lorcan
turns.text: Three years of being eighteen to twenty-one somewhere unfamiliar does something that two years does less of.

turns.speaker: Mimi
turns.text: Although that argument is much easier to make if nobody in your family is waiting for you to start earning.

turns.speaker: Gus
turns.text: Which is the whole pattern with this. The objections are all real and all come from comfortable places.

turns.speaker: Lorcan
turns.text: I'd accept that. My preference would be offering both rather than replacing one with the other.

turns.speaker: Mimi
turns.text: The risk there is that the two-year version becomes the one poorer students take, and employers learn to read it.

points: Two-year degrees are being piloted using three terms a year rather than two.
Mimi notes this saves a year of living costs, which exceed fees as the real expense.
Lorcan argues the loss is summer opportunities such as internships, paid work and research placements, which vary in importance by subject.
A maturing argument favours three years, though Mimi observes it is easier to make when family finances allow it.
Gus notes the objections are genuine but tend to come from comfortable positions.
Lorcan would offer both; Mimi warns the shorter version could become the poorer students' route and be read as inferior by employers.
